title: MCP in 2026: Linux Foundation Governance and the Stateless Redesign
content:
## Overview

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) — introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 — went through its biggest structural changes to date over the past year: a governance handoff away from Anthropic, and a ground-up protocol redesign now in release-candidate form. This page covers what changed and why it matters for anyone building or running MCP servers.

---

## Governance: MCP Leaves Anthropic's Sole Control

In December 2025, Anthropic donated MCP to the **Agentic AI Foundation**, a new body under the **Linux Foundation**. This made MCP a vendor-neutral, community-governed standard rather than an Anthropic-owned spec — the same maturation path other widely-adopted infra standards (Kubernetes, OpenTelemetry) have followed. A formal deprecation policy now accompanies the spec, so breaking changes go through a documented process instead of landing unannounced.

---

## The 2026-07-28 Release Candidate: A Stateless Core

The `2026-07-28` spec release candidate is described by the MCP team as the largest revision since launch. Its central change: MCP's core moves from a **stateful, session-oriented model** to a **stateless core that scales on ordinary HTTP infrastructure**.

Why this matters: the original MCP transport model (persistent stdio or SSE connections per client-server pair) works well for a single local client talking to a single local server, but scales poorly behind standard HTTP load balancers, since state has to stay pinned to one backend instance. A stateless core lets MCP servers be deployed like any other stateless HTTP API — horizontally scaled, load-balanced, and cached without sticky sessions.

The RC bundles this with two new extensions:

- **MCP Apps** — server-rendered UI, letting an MCP server return a renderable interface (not just data/tool results) that the host application displays
- **Tasks extension** — first-class support for long-running work, so a tool call that takes minutes or hours can be tracked and polled rather than forcing the connection to stay open

Authorization was also reworked to align more closely with standard **OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect** deployments, replacing bespoke auth flows from the original spec.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) Reaches Stable

The **Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)** extension — which gives organizations centralized control over which MCP servers their users/agents can reach, enforced through the org's existing identity provider — was promoted from draft to **stable** status in mid-2026. It has already been adopted by Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta, among a growing list of MCP servers. This addresses a common enterprise blocker: before EMA, admins had no standard way to restrict which MCP servers a Claude Code or Claude Desktop user could connect to org-wide.

---

## Ecosystem Growth

MCP server adoption continued to broaden through 2026. Notably, **X (formerly Twitter)** shipped a hosted MCP server in June 2026 that lets MCP-compatible clients — Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, and others — call the X API using a user's own account permissions, rather than requiring a separate developer API key setup. This kind of "first-party hosted MCP server" pattern (as opposed to a community-built wrapper) is becoming more common as platforms recognize MCP as the default integration surface for AI agents.

---

## What This Means for Builders

- **Server authors:** plan for the stateless transport model if you're building for scale — sticky-session assumptions baked into early MCP servers will need revisiting.
- **Enterprises:** EMA is now a viable answer to "how do we govern which MCP servers our agents can reach," rather than an ad hoc allowlist per tool.
- **Everyone:** the deprecation policy means future breaking changes should come with advance notice — check the MCP blog's roadmap posts before assuming stability of undocumented behavior.
